article: Why did cyclists in a beetroot trial get beetroot juice in both groups?
Read the nitrate-depleted comparator as part of the original cycling experiment.
Lansley et al. original cycling time-trial study using a nitrate-depleted beetroot comparison. No regimen guidance.
copy: A beetroot trial can compare a nitrate-containing drink with a nitrate-depleted drink derived from beetroot. That is different from comparing a beetroot drink against plain water. The purpose of the comparator is to bring more of the background drink into both conditions while changing nitrate exposure.
Read what the control leaves in and takes out

Check how well the paper describes the two drinks and what happened during the exercise tests. A similar color and taste help answer one design question, while a verified nitrate difference answers another. The measured result belongs to the tested conditions and does not establish an effect for any red-colored juice.
When summarizing the result, identify both drinks and say which exercise test the researchers used.

article: Did a caffeine gum study find quicker absorption or a greater total amount absorbed?
Separate the concentration timeline from exposure across the measurement window.
Original human caffeine gum and capsule pharmacokinetic comparison. No usage schedule.
copy: An original caffeine study compared chewing gum with capsules and reported how quickly caffeine appeared in measured samples. A faster concentration rise is a statement about timing. It is separate from comparing the amount of exposure over the entire sampling window.
Read the time variable and the total exposure separately

Look for outcomes such as time to peak and the area under the concentration curve. One compares when a high reading occurred, while the other summarizes exposure over time. Neither automatically tells you the effect of a different gum, amount, capsule or other ingredients.
Use the actual formulation and follow-up period when quoting the experiment. The study does not define when an individual should take caffeine.

article: Does tingling after beta-alanine show that a workout will improve?
Read a formulation study that measured sensations and absorption without treating tingling as performance.
Original slow-release beta-alanine kinetics study and separate exercise-capacity trial. No dosing guidance.
copy: A beta-alanine kinetics study measured absorption-related variables and reported paresthesia, a tingling sensation. That report can compare how participants felt under tested conditions. Tingling does not act as a direct meter for cycling, lifting or another performance outcome.
Look for a performance test rather than a sensation

A different exercise study can report what participants actually did under a specific test. Do not combine the findings into a claim that more tingling predicts better results. The participants, formulations and measured endpoints can all differ. A noticeable sensation might also help participants guess which condition they received.
Read the outcome next to the actual comparison. Do not use an adverse sensation to decide whether a product has worked.

article: What did a bicarbonate cycling experiment test about expectations?
Read the difference between actual assignment, expected benefits and the cycling result in a placebo experiment.
Original cycling placebo/nocebo and enteric-coated bicarbonate trials. No preparation or dosing instructions.
copy: A bicarbonate cycling study examined expectations as well as the actual substance. That matters because knowing or guessing the assigned condition can influence effort and how people report their experience. The measured blood response and exercise performance are separate outcomes.
Keep the instructions to participants with their outcome

When reading a claim, ask what each group received and what participants thought they received. A treatment result can look different under different instructions. Also check whether physical symptoms could have revealed the condition even when the study intended to mask it.
Do not use the study to set a personal bicarbonate routine. It helps explain why an experiment must report how it handled expectation.

article: Can extra seconds in a lab exhaustion test predict a faster ride over a fixed distance?
Compare two original cycling protocols by their finish rule rather than equating their time results.
Primary cycling time-to-exhaustion and 4 km time-trial studies of bicarbonate-related interventions. No regimen guidance.
copy: A time-to-exhaustion protocol measures how long a participant can keep going under specified demands before reaching the test’s stop condition. A fixed-distance time trial measures how quickly a participant completes the distance. Both may report seconds, but they use different end points.
Check what ends each test

In a time trial the participant may change pace during the effort. A fixed-demand protocol tests how long they sustain a workload. A percentage difference in one design cannot be copied directly into the other. Find the distance or demand, comparator and rules for the test before quoting its results.
Use the correct direction when reading the table. More time can be favorable in one design and less time in the other.

article: Does a BCAA trial measure muscle protein synthesis or long-term muscle growth?
Read an original tracer study by its measurement window and comparator.
Original acute muscle protein synthesis and BCAA-fortification studies. No recommendations on supplement use.
copy: A BCAA study can measure changes in how quickly muscle makes protein over a controlled period after exercise. That is different from measuring change in muscle size or strength after months of training. The original acute study reports an outcome for a specified sample, session and comparator.
Keep the measurement window in the headline

Comparison matters as much as timing. A BCAA drink compared with placebo tests a different question from adding BCAAs to a food or comparing with a larger quantity of intact protein. Check the meal background and the exact intervention before transferring the result to a different product.
Report the lab outcome alongside its duration. A short-term synthesis rate cannot identify the amount of muscle a particular person will gain.

article: Why can a supplement trial report more incidents than people with side effects?
Read ClinicalTrials.gov results by events and participants at risk, using a worked example.
ClinicalTrials.gov reporting guidance. Hypothetical counts are used to distinguish event and participant denominators.
copy: If three people report seven events, people affected and events are different counts. A percentage of people affected needs the number of participants at risk. In an example with 20 participants at risk and three affected people, 15% reported one or more events. Seven events can include repeat reports from the same person.
Divide by the number the result actually describes

Read the event definition, collection window and whether the groups had comparable follow-up. Do not divide the event count by the number of people and describe it as the proportion who had a symptom. Separate serious adverse events, other adverse events and reasons for leaving a study.
Check the actual results table when a report says a product was well tolerated.

article: Does a new dietary ingredient notification mean an FDA-approved supplement?
Check what a U.S. notification is filed for and what a seller’s approval claim would need to show.
U.S. FDA new dietary ingredient notification process and supplement regulatory overview.
copy: Some dietary supplements involving a new dietary ingredient require a notification to the FDA before marketing. A notification concerns the identified new ingredient and use conditions described in the submission. The filing does not amount to approval of the finished supplement, and it does not show that advertised benefits were tested.
Read the notification in its exact scope

If a seller cites a filing, check the applicable ingredient identity and the original record. The presence of a submission or a company claim about it does not tell you that a different formula, serving or intended use was evaluated. Review the actual correspondence where available.
Keep the regulatory step separate from research supporting a claimed effect.

article: Why does one similar-looking drink use Supplement Facts and another Nutrition Facts?
Read FDA beverage guidance and compare the product’s intended use and presentation.
FDA U.S. guidance on distinguishing liquid dietary supplements and beverages.
copy: Being liquid does not determine whether a product is sold as a beverage or a dietary supplement. FDA guidance considers how the product is represented, including the label, serving and recommended use. Two packages of similar size can carry different facts panels.
The bottle shape is only one clue

Check whether the label presents the product as a conventional drink or as a dietary supplement. If you are comparing a particular nutrient, use the declared amount for the labeled portion on each. A panel type does not establish that a similar flavor or packaging means a matching caffeine or sugar amount.
Keep the intended use and the measured quantity with the product whenever you compare them.

article: Does an NIH supplement label archive show what is in the bottle you just bought?
Use the Dietary Supplement Label Database as an archive and match its label to the actual package.
NIH ODS description of the U.S. Dietary Supplement Label Database.
copy: The NIH database catalogs information printed on supplement labels. It can help you find a label or see whether wording changed. A stored label does not establish that every package sold today uses the same formulation or that the declared ingredients were independently measured.
Check the exact product and label edition

Compare the brand, product name, package size and serving size with the bottle in front of you. Keep the database edition or access date when you use an archived record. If the amounts differ, use the label that applies to the package you actually have rather than averaging two editions.
This distinction also matters in research. A historical label can be exactly what the researcher needs without representing current stock.

article: Does a missing Daily Value mean an ingredient amount is missing?
Read the symbol beside supplement ingredients that have no established Daily Value.
U.S. FDA Supplement Facts guidance on ingredients without a reference Daily Value. Example amount is hypothetical.
copy: A supplement label can list the amount of an ingredient and use a symbol to show there is no established Daily Value for it. In an example, 200 mg describes the declared amount per serving even though there is no percentage in that row.
The weight and the reference are separate fields

Look for the symbol’s footnote and the full serving size. Do not turn a missing percentage into zero or try to substitute another nutrient’s reference. If an amount is also absent, check whether the label gives a blend total or another reason it cannot be determined.
Compare two products using the ingredient and declared units where possible. An absent Daily Value does not establish effectiveness, safety or the amount an individual needs.

article: What does the lot number tell you that a best-by date cannot?
Use FDA manufacturing guidance to distinguish a traceable batch from a date printed on a supplement.
U.S. FDA dietary supplement manufacturing-practice guidance. Label examples are hypothetical.
copy: A date and a lot number can appear near each other, but they do different things. A lot number identifies the batch for traceability. A best-by or expiration date, where present, describes a separate time-related statement. Two packages can show the same date without belonging to the same lot.
Copy the two fields separately

If you are checking a recall or quality notice, read the specified identifiers and match them exactly to the package. A bottle that looks identical on a shelf could come from another batch. Conversely, an intact lot number does not tell you how someone stored a bottle after purchase.
Keep the package and the current product label when querying the seller or regulator about a specific item.

article: Why does a supplement label put a second folate amount in parentheses?
Use NIH and FDA label examples to tell a dietary folate equivalent from the actual folic acid amount.
NIH folate fact sheet and FDA updated-label guidance. Illustrative 667 µg DFE (400 µg folic acid) declaration.
copy: In a U.S. supplement example, a label can state 667 µg DFE with 400 µg folic acid in parentheses. The DFE number expresses dietary folate equivalents. The figure in parentheses describes the actual stated amount of folic acid. They are two descriptions of the same declared ingredient contribution.
Read the parenthetical figure before comparing folic acid

Do not add the numbers or compare one product’s DFE figure with another product’s folic acid figure. Check the labeled serving and the form. A label that identifies a different folate form needs its own reading before you transfer an inference from a folic acid example.
Use the exact figure relevant to your comparison. This is label arithmetic rather than personal intake guidance.
